‘There’s nothing soft about relationship-based nursing skills’

29 September, 2026 By Madeline Siefert

Madeline Siefert
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:42
Instaread

When I first learned in my undergraduate nursing studies that trust establishment and building therapeutic nurse−patient relationships were considered soft skills.

I was immediately disappointed. Only recently, as a PhD student studying the nurse-patient relationship, did I ask myself why.

“When relationship-based skills are labeled as soft, it devalues a measurable driver of patient outcomes”

This language choice diminishes the critical importance of relationship-building in nursing, leading it to be viewed as less important than other nursing skills.

In nursing, hard skills are quantifiable, tangible skills and can be assessed for competency.

Soft skills, such as empathy demonstration and trust building, are not consistently standardised.

A scoping review assessing soft and hard skills in nursing education found difficulties in defining, teaching, and assessing soft skills because of the lack of standardisation.

Additionally, the importance placed on the development of hard skills in nursing is consistently greater than its soft counterpart.

I think the root of this imbalance is directly related to the verbiage chosen to differentiate the two skill sets. Our society’s categorisation of the word soft plays an impactful role.

When you search the Merriam-Webster Thesaurus for synonyms of ‘soft’, it provides categories for different definitions of the word, including one: ‘soft as in weak’.

Political discourse has led to the categorisation of individuals as snowflakes, a weak, fragile substance.

Similarly, feminist culture demands that women must constantly demonstrate strength to elicit change, leaving no room for weakness.

This categorisation of weakness as soft is not limited to our political world; it bleeds into all aspects of our society, and healthcare is no exception.

When relationship-based skills are labeled as soft, it devalues a measurable driver of patient outcomes and ultimately patient safety.

As a nursing leader, I check in with my nurses consistently. One question consistently asked is: “what is the most enjoyable aspect of your job?”

The recurring answer: talking and connecting with their patients. Building a relationship with patients matters to nurses.

However, there is a caveat. What they actually say is: “Talking and connecting with my patients, well, when I have time.”

The number of responsibilities a bedside nurse must complete in a 12-hour shift is daunting.

When tasks pile up and the clock keeps ticking, nurses must decide what gets done and what gets cut.

Nurses are forced to prioritise measured and audited tasks, and as a result, the relationship-building aspect of care is sacrificed.

Then, there is the perspective of patients. I ask our patients: “Are our nurses providing you excellent care?” When they respond with ‘yes’, it is never simply a ‘yes’.

It is asking for their nurse’s last name so they can nominate them for a Daisy Award, which recognises excellence in nursing.

It is shared through tears how thankful they are for the care they’ve received. This aligns with findings of a 2024 study in Enfermería Intensiva evaluating patient satisfaction, with the nurse−patient relationship as a major theme.

The American Nurses Association further supports the view that the nurse−patient relationship increases patient satisfaction and can reduce hospital length of stay.

So, what about when that doesn’t happen? Well, what happens to any individual after a negative encounter? They don’t forget. Our experiences shape us and our decision-making.

When patients tell me they are not receiving excellent care, it is almost always related to timeliness. Often, patients recognise the task demands nurses face.

However, when patients feel nurses don’t have time for them, they ask fewer questions, engage less in their own care, and may even take actions that could cause harm.

For example, a 2015 study in the Western Journal of Nursing Research, evaluating trust development between Mexican American patients and nurses, found that when patients felt a lack of trust, they would try to ambulate unassisted, increasing their risk for inpatient falls.

This indicates that trust is not abstract; it directly influences patient safety, a measurable patient outcome.

Ultimately, the hard-versus-soft-skills categorisation is simply that: a categorisation. I understand the differences in the categories and why they should be placed in separate boxes.

However, words matter. The current language places less value on relationship-building, which can inevitably lead to patient harm.

Task efficiency is consistently valued above relationship-building, even though it is vital to nursing and patient satisfaction.

So, let’s find a different word, because when we call something soft, it’s easier to ignore, and that’s a risk patients can’t afford.

Madeline Siefert is an assistant nurse manager in a surgical intensive care unit and a nursing PhD student

References

American Nurses Association (2023) Nurturing trust in the nurse-patient relationship.

García DJ et al (2025) Assessment of soft and hard skills in nursing and students nursing: A scoping review. Nurse Education in Practice, 89, 01-08.
